prompt: shared.py ends with minus one copy of Iracema. Which line of lend is wrong?

choices.text: The check, because it should test for more than one copy
choices.why: With one copy on the shelf, testing for more than one would refuse a loan that is allowed.

choices.text: None of them: the bug lives in the whole gap between the check and the act
choices.why: Right. Each line is correct; a second thread ran between them.

choices.text: The decrement, because -= on a dictionary is not allowed from a thread
choices.why: Any thread may write to the dictionary; that freedom is the problem, not a refusal.

prompt: Match each way out of the shared-state problem to what it does.

pairs.right: lets one thread at a time into the check-and-act
never changes shared data, only builds new values
gives the data one owner that others send messages to

prompt: Without the sleep, shared.py prints one lend and one refusal on every run you try. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The race only exists because of the sleep, so removing it fixes the program
choices.why: The sleep only widens the gap; the operating system can switch threads at the same point without it.

choices.text: Little: the bad interleaving is rare, and rare per run is frequent per day of use
choices.why: Right. A test that passes here proves nothing, which is why the fix is a design rule.

choices.text: Python runs threads one after the other, so they never overlap
choices.why: The run with the sleep shows them overlapping; the interpreter switches threads between steps.

prompt: A system holds a million actors on a machine with eight threads. How is that possible?

choices.text: It is not: each actor needs a thread of its own
choices.why: That confuses running code with owning state; an actor needs a thread only while it has messages.

choices.text: The actors share their state, so one thread can serve many at once
choices.why: Sharing state is exactly what actors never do; the threads are shared, the state is not.

choices.text: Most actors are idle; a thread is lent only while one has work
choices.why: Right. An actor is a way of owning state; the runtime lends it a thread when there is work.

prompt: While handling a message, which of these may an actor do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Send messages to actors whose address it knows
choices.why: Right. That is the first of Hewitt's three.

choices.text: Create new actors
choices.why: Right. That is the second.

choices.text: Read another actor's state directly, if it only reads
choices.why: Reading is still access; the other actor may be changing it at that instant.

choices.text: Decide how it will handle the next message
choices.why: Right. That is how an actor's state changes.

prompt: Messages for an actor wait in its ___ until it takes them out one at a time.
actor.py keeps the same time.sleep between check and act as shared.py. Why does the shelf no longer go below zero?

choices.text: The second Lend waits its turn in the mailbox
choices.why: Right. Only the actor's thread runs the check-and-act, one message at a time.

choices.text: queue.Queue takes a lock around the whole of receive
choices.why: The queue locks only its own put and get; receive is safe because a single thread runs it.

choices.text: The desks run one after the other in actor.py, not together
choices.why: They still run at the same moment; what they do at once is put a message in the queue.

prompt: In Shelf.__init__, why is super().__init__() the last line rather than the first?

choices.text: Python requires the parent constructor to be called last
choices.why: Python allows it anywhere; the order here is a choice with a reason.

choices.text: It starts the thread, and the state has to exist before that
choices.why: Right. Started first, the thread could take a message before _copies exists.

choices.text: So that the mailbox is empty when the copies are set
choices.why: The mailbox is made by the parent; the risk is the thread, not the queue.

choices.text: To let the subclass replace the mailbox with a bounded one
choices.why: Nothing in Shelf touches the mailbox.

prompt: The north desk sends Lend and the south desk sends GiveBack at the same moment. In which order does the shelf receive them?

choices.text: Lend first, because commands to take come before commands to return
choices.why: The mailbox knows nothing about meaning; it keeps arrival order.

choices.text: Alphabetically by desk, because the queue sorts its senders
choices.why: A queue never sorts; it is first in, first out.

choices.text: Whichever arrives first; order is only promised per sender
choices.why: Right. A design needing that order makes one sender wait for the other.

prompt: Why does the shelf not simply get a method available(title) that returns the count?

choices.text: It would read _copies from the caller's thread, the wrong one
choices.why: Right. The answer has to come from the actor's own thread, so it comes back as a message.

choices.text: Methods cannot return values from a class that inherits from Actor
choices.why: They can; the problem is which thread runs the method.

choices.text: A method call would be slower than sending a message
choices.why: A call is faster; it is unsafe, which matters more.

prompt: Handling Recount, the shelf asks itself and times out after 0.5 s. Why would no answer ever come?

choices.text: Available is not a message the shelf knows how to handle
choices.why: CountingShelf handles Available; the main thread's asks were answered.

choices.text: Only the shelf's thread answers, and that thread is the one waiting
choices.why: Right. The question sits in the mailbox behind the message being handled.

choices.text: Futures cannot be passed inside a frozen dataclass
choices.why: Frozen means the field cannot be reassigned; the future inside still works, as the first asks show.

prompt: A desk lends a book by telling, with no ask. Put the steps in order.
items: The desk tells the shelf: lend Iracema to Bia, and reply to me
The shelf checks and takes a copy in one step
The shelf tells the desk Lent or Refused
The desk handles the reply as its next message
trap: Asking first whether a copy is free and then telling the shelf to lend reopens the gap between check and act.

prompt: In supervision.py, Iracema starts with 2 copies and is lent twice, with a crash and restart in between. How many copies does the shelf report after the second loan?
A restarted shelf forgot a loan. What does the section say should change?

choices.text: The supervisor should copy the old shelf's state into the new one
choices.why: The old state is the state that led to the crash; restarting clean is the point.

choices.text: State that must survive a crash belongs somewhere durable
choices.why: Right. A database or an event log the new instance replays, as in lesson 9.

choices.text: The shelf should catch every exception so that it never needs a restart
choices.why: That is the defensive code the section argues against: running on in states nobody designed.

prompt: A member types a title the library does not hold. How should the shelf actor respond?

choices.text: Crash, so that the supervisor restarts it with a clean state
choices.why: A typo is expected input; crashing would spend a restart and lose state for nothing.

choices.text: Ignore the message, since it cannot be handled
choices.why: Ignoring it is a silent failure: the member waits for an answer that never comes.

choices.text: With an ordinary reply saying there is no such title
choices.why: Right. Validate expected problems at the edge; let the inside crash on the impossible.

prompt: In location.py, ref.tell(threading.Lock()) raises TypeError at once. What does that show?

choices.text: A message must become bytes, so shared state cannot travel
choices.why: Right. The rule that messages are values becomes something the transport enforces.

choices.text: The shelf process refused the lock because it already holds one
choices.why: The shelf never saw it: the error came from pickling on the sending side.

choices.text: Ref.tell only accepts frozen dataclasses
choices.why: Ref.tell sends whatever it is given; None goes through at the end.

prompt: Why does an ask without a timeout become more dangerous once the actor runs on another machine?

choices.text: Remote actors answer more slowly, so the default wait is too short
choices.why: There is no wait limit at all without a timeout; that is the danger.

choices.text: A lost reply now makes it hang, not just a bug
choices.why: Right. Networks lose messages, and a silent machine looks like a slow one.

choices.text: Futures cannot cross a network, so the ask fails at once
choices.why: Remote systems use a reply address that can cross; the failure is the wait, not the send.

choices.text: The remote supervisor cancels every ask when it restarts the actor
choices.why: Nothing cancels the ask; the caller just waits for a reply that will not come.

prompt: A desk retries GiveBack when no acknowledgement arrives in two seconds. What must the shelf's handler be?

choices.text: Faster than two seconds, so the retry never happens
choices.why: A lost acknowledgement triggers the retry however fast the handler was.

choices.text: Supervised by the desk, so that the desk can restart it
choices.why: Supervision handles crashes; it does nothing about a message arriving twice.

choices.text: Idempotent: the same return handled twice must count once
choices.why: Right. A retry after a lost acknowledgement delivers the message twice.

prompt: What separates a goroutine reading a channel from an actor with a mailbox?

choices.text: A goroutine cannot hold state between messages
choices.why: The shelf goroutine keeps its map across requests; that is what makes it actor-like.

choices.text: The channel is shared, and a send waits for a receiver
choices.why: Right. An actor has the address, and its tell never waits.

choices.text: Goroutines run in separate processes with separate memory
choices.why: Goroutines share one process's memory; Erlang's processes are the ones with separate memory.

prompt: In the Akka example, the Lend handler returns shelf(withOneLess(copies, ...)) instead of changing a field. Which idea is that?

choices.text: Choosing the behaviour for the next message, with the state built new
choices.why: Right. Hewitt's third rule, written literally, with lesson 15's immutability.

choices.text: Restarting the actor after every message, as a supervisor would
choices.why: Nothing failed; returning a behaviour is the normal path, and the new state carries the loan.

choices.text: Recursion that grows the stack with each message until it overflows
choices.why: The function returns a description of the next behaviour; Akka calls it later, so no stack builds up.

prompt: supervision.py is run again with max_restarts=3 and the same six messages. How many of them change the shelf's copies?
hint: The three GiveBacks of unknown titles crash; now none of them exhausts the limit.

prompt: A loans actor asks the members actor whether a member may borrow, and the members actor asks the loans actor how many books she holds. What happens under load?

choices.text: Nothing bad: each actor handles one message at a time, so no race is possible
choices.why: No race inside each actor, but each can block waiting on the other: that is a deadlock, not a race.

choices.text: Each one waits on the other, and both stop handling their mailboxes
choices.why: Right. Two actors asking each other deadlock; tell with a reply address avoids it.

choices.text: The supervisor notices the slow replies and restarts both actors
choices.why: A supervisor reacts to crashes; a blocked actor has not crashed, unless a timeout turns the hang into an error.

choices.text: Messages are dropped once each mailbox reaches its default size
choices.why: The default mailboxes here are unbounded; they grow while both actors wait.

prompt: The kiosks and both desks update a count of visitors today, and it comes out too low at closing time. Which fix matches this lesson?

choices.text: Read the count twice before writing it, to check that nobody changed it
choices.why: Another writer can still run between the second read and the write; the gap only moves.

choices.text: One counter actor owns the count, and everyone tells it Visited
choices.why: Right. Only one thread changes the count, so no update is lost.

choices.text: Give each kiosk its own copy of the count and let them overwrite the total
choices.why: Overwriting the total loses every other writer's increments, which is the bug itself.
